**Solution 1 (185) is the most likely to be correct, though its lower-bound argument is flawed.**

**Reduction.** Fix a pair of primes p ≠ q. Given the observed values y on S = {x₁,…,xₙ}, the values are consistent with a nonconstant p-periodic function iff y is constant on residue classes mod p, and, when S covers every residue mod p, y is not constant. Build a graph on S with edges between elements that share a residue mod p or mod q. Ambiguity between p and q arises exactly when this graph is disconnected (a nonconstant y is then valid for both) or when it is connected but S misses a residue mod p and also a residue mod q (the constant y is valid for both). So Ana wins for {p, q} iff the bipartite graph on Z_p ∪ Z_q with an edge for each xᵢ is connected on its used vertices, and S covers all residues mod p or all mod q.

**Consequences.**
- At most one prime below 100 can have an incomplete residue cover, since every pair needs one fully covered prime.
- If two primes p, q are both fully covered, the bipartite graph uses all p + q vertices, so n ≥ p + q − 1.
- Excluding 97 as the uncovered prime forces the pair (89, 83), giving n ≥ 171. This is a sharper lower bound than 185, so Solution 1's claim that the maximum over all pairs gives the bound is not justified.

**Other solutions.**
- Solution 2 (98) is wrong. Covering every residue mod 97 alone requires at least 97 points, and pairs of primes force many more.
- Solution 3 (186) rests on an interval-of-integers argument with no real lower-bound proof. Its non-existence claim for n < 186 is unsupported.

I could not fully determine the true minimum. My own lower bound of 171 suggests the answer may lie below 185, but the tree-like constraints across all pairs simultaneously are not resolved here. Among the three proposed values, 185 is the one that follows from the correct connectivity framework, while 98 and 186 do not.

CHOICE: 1
